import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Asymptotic density of powerful numbers

Let $Q(x)$ denote the number of powerful integers up to $x$. Erdős and Szekeres [ES35] proved
$$Q(x) = \frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)} x^{1/2} + O(x^{1/3}),$$
and Bateman and Grosswald [BG58] sharpened this to
$$Q(x) = \frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)} x^{1/2} + \frac{\zeta(2/3)}{\zeta(2)} x^{1/3} + O(x^{1/6}).$$
Improving the exponent $1/6$ in the error term unconditionally remains open; conditional
improvements are known under the Riemann Hypothesis.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powerful_number)
- [ES35] Erdős, P. and Szekeres, G., *Über die Anzahl der Abelschen Gruppen gegebener Ordnung
  und über ein verwandtes zahlentheoretisches Problem*, Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged) 7 (1935), 95–102.
- [BG58] Bateman, P. T. and Grosswald, E., *On a theorem of Erdős and Szekeres*,
  Illinois J. Math. 2 (1958), 88–98.
-/

open Filter Asymptotics Real

namespace PowerfulNumbersDensity

/-- $Q(x)$ is the number of powerful integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le x$. -/
noncomputable abbrev Q (x : ℝ) : ℕ := {n : ℕ | 0 < n ∧ n.Powerful ∧ (n : ℝ) ≤ x}.ncard

/-- The leading constant $\zeta(3/2)/\zeta(3) = 2.173\ldots$ -/
noncomputable abbrev A : ℝ := (riemannZeta (3 / 2)).re / (riemannZeta 3).re

/-- The second-order constant $\zeta(2/3)/\zeta(2)$, where $\zeta(2/3)$ is given by analytic
continuation. -/
noncomputable abbrev B : ℝ := (riemannZeta (2 / 3)).re / (riemannZeta 2).re

/--
Erdős and Szekeres [ES35] proved that the number of powerful integers up to $x$ satisfies
$$Q(x) = \frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)} x^{1/2} + O(x^{1/3}).$$
In particular $Q(x) \sim \frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)} \sqrt{x}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem asymptotic_erdos_szekeres :
    (fun x : ℝ => (Q x : ℝ) - A * x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 2)) =O[atTop]
      fun x => x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 3) := by
  sorry

/--
Bateman and Grosswald [BG58] proved the sharper asymptotic
$$Q(x) = \frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)} x^{1/2} + \frac{\zeta(2/3)}{\zeta(2)} x^{1/3} + O(x^{1/6}).$$
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem asymptotic_bateman_grosswald :
    (fun x : ℝ => (Q x : ℝ) - A * x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 2) - B * x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 3)) =O[atTop]
      fun x => x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 6) := by
  sorry

/--
Can the exponent $1/6$ in the error term of the Bateman–Grosswald asymptotic be improved
unconditionally? That is, is there $\delta > 0$ such that
$$Q(x) = \frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)} x^{1/2} + \frac{\zeta(2/3)}{\zeta(2)} x^{1/3} +
O(x^{1/6 - \delta})?$$
Improvements are known under the Riemann Hypothesis.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem error_term_improvement :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ δ > (0 : ℝ),
      (fun x : ℝ => (Q x : ℝ) - A * x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 2) - B * x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 3)) =O[atTop]
        fun x => x ^ ((1 : ℝ) / 6 - δ) := by
  sorry

end PowerfulNumbersDensity

findings.description: The declaration records only E(x) = O(x^(1/6)), where E(x) = Q(x) − A*x^(1/2) − B*x^(1/3). The cited Bateman–Grosswald result gives E(x) = o(x^(1/6)), and their Theorem 3 gives an even stronger quantitative remainder. These conditions are not equivalent: the Lean statement requires the normalized error merely to be bounded, rather than to tend to zero. I verified the distinction in Lean using the generic residual x^(1/6), which is big-O but not little-o of itself. The displayed estimate is nevertheless a true weaker corollary and is sufficient to establish the baseline for the following open question, so deliberately retaining it is defensible; the concern is presenting this weakening as the Bateman–Grosswald asymptotic without identifying it as a coarse version.
findings.source_evidence: Bateman and Grosswald, “On a theorem of Erdős and Szekeres,” Illinois J. Math. 2 (1958), §5, pp. 94–95: “In particular the simple estimate M(n) = o(n), which is equivalent to the prime number theorem, gives an error term o(x^(1/6)).” Theorem 3 supplies a stronger subexponential saving. DOI: 10.1215/ijm/1255380836; primary-paper text read through https://r.jina.ai/https://projecteuclid.org/journals/illinois-journal-of-mathematics/volume-2/issue-1/On-a-theorem-of-Erd%C3%B6s-and-Szekeres/10.1215/ijm/1255380836.pdf . The Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry linked from Wikipedia explicitly displays N₂(x) = A*x^(1/2) + B*x^(1/3) + o(x^(1/6)): https://encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php?title=Power-full_number .
findings.suggested_fix: If this declaration is intended to record the standard Bateman–Grosswald asymptotic, replace `=O[atTop]` by `=o[atTop]` and update the corresponding formulas in the docstrings. Alternatively, explicitly identify the existing theorem as a deliberately weakened corollary; the subsequent fixed-power-saving question need not change.

reformulations.difference: The original Erdős–Szekeres paper uses an integer cutoff n. Lean states the asymptotic for a real cutoff x and uses `atTop` rather than an explicit positivity restriction.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For x ≥ 1, put n = floor(x). Then Q(x) = Q(n), n ≤ x < n+1, and |sqrt(x) − sqrt(n)| ≤ 1. Thus an integer-cutoff error bound C*n^(1/3) gives a real-cutoff bound (C+|A|)*x^(1/3) eventually. The converse follows by restricting to integer arguments. Nonpositive real arguments are irrelevant at `atTop`. The exact floor identity and the eventual-bound interpretation of big-O were proved in the scratch file, though not the complete integer/real equivalence.

reformulations.difference: Bateman–Grosswald discuss an estimate with a fixed exponent α < 1/6; Lean expresses this as a positive saving δ, with exponent 1/6 − δ and no upper bound on δ.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Set α = 1/6 − δ in one direction and δ = 1/6 − α in the other. Both transformations preserve the bound exactly. Nor is an upper bound on δ missing: any witness δ can be replaced by min(δ,1/12), since increasing the exponent weakens the big-O bound for x ≥ 1. Both equivalences were proved in Lean for an arbitrary real-valued residual function.

review.notes: All six declarations were checked. `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` compiles without errors and verifies finiteness of the set counted by Q for every real x, the positive-integer powerful predicate, Q at negative and small cutoffs (including Q(100)=14), the complex rational arguments and real-valued zeta quotients, positive denominators, and the quantifier interpretation of the asymptotic bounds. The helper proofs do not use the file's sorry-backed theorems. No definite misformalization or stale status was found. In particular, the known unconditional subexponential improvement is not a fixed power saving, and the recent arXiv paper's additional zero-residue terms do not settle the stated open question. The target file was not modified.
